Not yet: this pilot does not establish that Fibonacci sequences or Phi Ratio improve binding prediction around OXTR. M9 P24 Alpha, Beta, Gamma and Epsilon were not evaluated for biological prediction in the new classical test. The laboratory evidence covers CTCF, one DNA-binding protein, in one stem-cell context—not transcription factors generally.

The agent completed a classical comparison of familiar DNA binding patterns and their spacing, with and without Fibonacci/Phi Ratio features. It learned on chromosome 1, chose the method on chromosome 2 and tested 152 OXTR windows on chromosome 3: it did not see OXTR laboratory answers while learning. The agent also prepared a new matched pair of DNA windows, one overlapping a reported CTCF peak and one comparison window, compiled all eight representations for each and completed 16 local CUDA-Q CPU checks. These are the same DNA prepared as ordinary, Fibonacci, Phi Ratio, Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Epsilon and shuffled controls.

Average precision, a ranking score rather than percent accuracy, changed from 0.0719 to 0.0739. The estimated uncertainty range for that change was −0.0263 to +0.0082, spanning both harm and benefit. This noisy change leaves benefit unresolved. The small pilot covers five OXTR peak regions and has laboratory quality warnings. Saved CUDA-Q/Aquila readings measure programmed quantum responses, not binding probabilities; the saved Aquila samples miss those peak regions and cannot validate binding prediction. The new pair checks programs, not predictive performance.
